{{Short description|Averages of functions under the Dirichlet distribution}}
'''Dirichlet averages''' are averages of functions under the [[Dirichlet distribution]]. An important one are dirichlet averages that have a certain argument structure, namely

<math display="block"> F(\mathbf{b};\mathbf{z})=\int f( \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{z}) \, d \mu_b(\mathbf{u}), </math>

where <math>\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{z}=\sum_i^N u_i \cdot z_i</math> and <math>d \mu_b(\mathbf{u})=u_1^{b_1-1} \cdots u_N^{b_N-1} d\mathbf{u}</math> is the Dirichlet measure with dimension&nbsp;''N''. They were introduced by the mathematician Bille C. Carlson in the '70s who noticed that the simple notion of this type of averaging generalizes and unifies many special functions, among them generalized [[hypergeometric function]]s or various [[orthogonal polynomials]]:.<ref name=Carlson1977>{{cite book |last1=Carlson |first1=B.C.|year=1977|title=Special functions of applied mathematics}}</ref> They also play an important role for the solution of [[elliptic integral]]s (see [[Carlson symmetric form]]) and are connected to statistical applications in various ways, for example in [[Bayesian analysis]].<ref name=Dickey1984>{{cite journal |last1=Dickey |first1=J.M.|year=1983|title=Multiple hypergeometric functions: Probabilistic interpretations and statistical uses.|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=78 |issue=383|pages=628–637 |doi=10.2307/2288131|jstor=2288131 }}</ref>

== Notable Dirichlet averages ==
Some Dirichlet averages are so fundamental that they are named. A few are listed below.

===R-function===

The (Carlson) R-function is the Dirichlet average of <math>x^n</math>,

<math display="block">R_n(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{z})=\int (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{z})^n \, d \mu_b(\mathbf{u})</math>

with <math>n </math>. Sometimes <math>R_n(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{z})</math> is also denoted by <math>R(-n;\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{z})</math>.

Exact solutions:

For <math>n \geq 0, n \in \mathbb{N}</math> it is possible to write an exact solution in the form of an iterative sum<ref name=Gluesenkamp2018>{{cite journal |last1=Glüsenkamp |first1=T.|year=2018|title=Probabilistic treatment of the uncertainty from the finite size of weighted Monte Carlo data |journal=EPJ Plus |volume=133 |issue=6|pages=218|doi=10.1140/epjp/i2018-12042-x |arxiv=1712.01293|bibcode=2018EPJP..133..218G }}</ref>

<math display="block">R_n(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{z})=\frac{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(b+n)} \cdot D_n \text{ with } D_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \left(\sum_{i=1}^N b_i \cdot z_i^k\right) \cdot D_{n-k}</math>

where <math>D_0=1</math>, <math>N</math> is the dimension of <math>\mathbf{b}</math> or <math>\mathbf{z}</math> and <math>b=\sum b_i</math>.

===S-function===
The (Carlson) S-function is the Dirichlet average of <math>e^x</math>,

<math display="block">S(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{z})=\int \exp(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{z}) \, d \mu_b(\mathbf{u}). </math>
